property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets C.owner() to the provided newOwner; the mutant instead clears owner to address(0) for some (most) inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in C.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that assigns address(0) instead will violate this for some fuzzed newOwner addresses.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates the contract's owner to newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment breaks this because owner remains unchanged after the call for some newOwner values.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address (different from the caller), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates the public owner getter to equal newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment breaks this because owner remains the old owner for some newOwner inputs.

For any address newOwner different from the current owner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner becomes newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment breaks this because owner remains the old owner for some newOwner inputs.

For any address newOwner that is not the zero address, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner becomes newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment violates this because owner remains the old owner for some newOwner inputs.

For any caller address X, in the correct contract only the initial owner (the deployer) can change owner via transferOwnership, so after any transferOwnership attempt by X the owner equals the deployer unless X is the deployer; the mutant (which removes the require) allows some non-deployer X to change owner so the property can be violated for some fuzzed X.

For all callers, only the contract deployer (initial owner) can successfully change owner via transferOwnership; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner check allows some non-deployer caller to change owner, violating this invariant for some input caller address.
Calling owned() as the owner never changes the owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so for some caller the owner will change after calling owned(), violating owner invariance.

For any caller X, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner (owner remains the same); the mutant sets owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so when X != original owner the owner will incorrectly change.

For any caller who is the current owner, invoking owned() does not change the contract's owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so after calling owned() the owner can change (to msg.sender) breaking that invariant for some fuzzed initial owner/caller combinations.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling owned() must NOT change the contract's owner (owner remains equal to the caller); the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so for some initial owner/caller combinations the owner will incorrectly change and the property is violated.

For any address initialOwner and any caller actor (where initialOwner != address(0)), after setting owner to initialOwner and then calling owned() as that owner, the contract's owner remains equal to initialOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner and thus violates this invariant for some inputs.
Calling owned() (which is onlyOwner) must NOT change the owner; the mutant breaks this by setting owner to msg.sender inside owned(), so for some caller the owner value changes after the call.

For any caller x, calling owned() (which requires caller == owner) does not change c.owner(); the mutant violates this because it assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so after owned() the owner may become the caller.

For every address a, calling owned() as a (i.e. msg.sender == owner) never changes c.owner(); the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so there exist inputs where c.owner() changes after the call.

For any address caller that is equal to c.owner(), invoking owned() does not change c.owner() (the owner remains the same); the mutant that calls transferOwnership(msg.sender) inside owned() can change owner to the caller, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every address a that is the current owner, calling owned() as a does not change c.owner() (the owner remains equal to the original owner); the mutant that calls transferOwnership(msg.sender) inside owned() can change owner to msg.sender and thus breaks this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller who is currently owner, calling owned() must NOT change the stored owner address; the mutant's modifier that assigns owner = msg.sender mutates owner during owned() and thus can change it.

For any caller address, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner (owner remains equal to its pre-call value); the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside the modifier, so for some callers this call will change owner and violate the rule.

For any caller address, invoking owned() (which requires the caller to be the current owner) does not change the contract's owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside the modifier, so calling owned() with an address that is not the initial owner but becomes owner via prior transfer can make the mutant change owner and violate the rule.

For any two distinct addresses A (initial owner) and B (caller), if ownership is transferred from A to B and then B calls owned(), the owner remains B afterwards (reference preserves owner across a modifier-only call; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender in the modifier can break this by changing owner during the call).

Calling owned() as the current owner never changes the owner state: for every caller who is equal to the contract's owner before the call, after calling owned() the owner remains the same; the mutant's modifier that assigns owner = msg.sender can introduce a spurious state change and thus violate this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller, invoking owned() does not change the contract's owner (owner remains equal to the original owner); the mutant incorrectly updates owner to tx.origin inside the onlyOwner modifier, so for some caller inputs the owner value will change after calling owned().
